opus-5.5.text:
Working through that survey really reshaped how I think about the whole field. Before, I had this somewhat romantic picture of AI for math: you train a big model, it reads a lot of papers, and eventually it starts producing proofs the way a mathematician would. Going through the literature carefully, I came to appreciate that the real bottleneck isn't just generating plausible-sounding mathematics. It's verification.

Informal math, the way we write it in papers, is full of gaps that a human expert fills in automatically. A language model can produce something that looks like a proof, and it can be very convincing, but there's no cheap way to know whether it's actually correct. Formal systems like Lean change that completely. Once a proof is written in a formal language, the kernel either accepts it or it doesn't. That gives you a perfectly reliable reward signal, which matters enormously if you want to do reinforcement learning, search, or self-improvement at scale.

The second thing I came to appreciate is how much infrastructure matters. A lot of progress came not from a single clever model but from the ecosystem: libraries like Mathlib, benchmarks, tooling that lets a model interact with the proof assistant step by step, and the work of autoformalization, translating natural-language math into formal statements. That last piece turned out to be one of the hardest and most underrated problems. If you can't faithfully state the theorem, proving it doesn't mean much.

And third, it changed my sense of what the end goal is. I used to think of it as "AI solving competition problems." Now I see it more as building a system where humans and machines collaborate: the mathematician supplies intuition and direction, and the machine handles rigor, checks details, and explores many paths in parallel. Formal verification is what makes that trust possible. So for me the survey turned AI for math from an impressive demo into something closer to a new scientific infrastructure, and that's a much more exciting frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says the survey reshaped the speaker’s view and describes several lessons, but it does not say that previously isolated knowledge of AI-for-math approaches came together into a coherent picture.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, that survey changed how I think about the whole field, in three ways.

First, it forced me to confront how early we really are. When I started, I thought formal theorem proving was mostly a question of scaling, that if you throw a big enough model at Lean or Isabelle, the proofs will come. Going paper by paper through the literature, you see that the actual bottleneck is not raw reasoning but the interface between informal mathematical intuition and the formal system. Humans do mathematics in a kind of compressed, sloppy, high-level language, and the proof assistant demands every detail. Autoformalization, translating natural-language statements into correct formal ones, turned out to be a much harder and much more important problem than I had appreciated. If you get the statement wrong, a perfect proof is worthless.

Second, it made me take the data problem seriously. Mathlib is wonderful, but it is tiny compared to what language models are used to. A lot of the most interesting work in the survey was really about how to manufacture signal: synthetic conjectures, proof search traces, retrieval over premise libraries, reinforcement learning where the verifier is the reward. That reframing was important for me. In this domain, you actually have a perfect oracle. The proof either checks or it does not. That is a rare gift in machine learning, and the question becomes how to exploit it efficiently rather than how to approximate ground truth.

Third, and this is the part that stayed with me, it shifted my view of what "AI for math" is even for. I went in thinking the goal was to prove famous open problems. I came out thinking the nearer-term value is infrastructure: making formalization cheap enough that working mathematicians can verify their own papers, build on each other's results without re-deriving everything, and trust a shared library. Formal proof as a kind of compiler for mathematics. The headline-grabbing results will come, but the quiet thing, making mathematics machine-checkable at scale, is what I now think the survey was really pointing toward.

So I would say it made me more humble about timelines and more excited about the problem. The hard parts are more interesting than I expected.

astra-6.text:
It helped me see AI for math as more than getting the right answer to a difficult problem. There’s also the question of how you represent the problem, find a proof, and check that every step actually follows.

Formal theorem proving gives you a powerful way to separate those tasks. An AI can propose an argument, and a proof assistant can check it against precise rules. But that doesn’t make the creative part disappear. Choosing a useful definition, finding the right intermediate lemma, or deciding which approach to pursue can still be the hardest part.

So the shift for me was toward thinking about the whole process: how informal mathematical intuition connects to formal, checkable reasoning. The exciting possibility is a system that helps explore ideas while giving us a reliable way to verify what it produces.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward viewing AI for math as a whole process, but does not say that the survey connected previously isolated knowledge of approaches into a coherent picture of the field.

sol-6.1.text:
Working through the survey helped me separate two things that are easy to conflate: finding a mathematical argument and formally verifying that argument. A proof can be convincing to a mathematician while still leaving a lot of work before a proof assistant will accept it. That gap became much more central to how I thought about AI for math.

It also made me appreciate the feedback loop that formal systems offer. A model can propose a step, the proof assistant can check it, and that feedback can guide the next attempt. But verification doesn’t tell you which definition to introduce or which intermediate lemma will make a problem tractable. Those choices still require mathematical judgment.

So I came away thinking less about whether AI could produce a polished proof in one shot, and more about how learning, search, and verification could work together—and how those systems could become useful collaborators for mathematicians.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinguishing proof discovery from formal verification and seeing how learning, search, and verification can work together. It does not state that the survey connected previously isolated knowledge of AI-for-math approaches into a coherent picture of the field.
